title: Civil claim instructions, historic abuse by swimming coach (synthetic)
setting: A solicitor takes first instructions from Matthew Kerr, 41, by video call, about a possible civil claim for abuse by his swimming coach at Harbridge Swimming Club in the 1990s.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Hi Matthew, can you hear me okay?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Yeah, I can hear you. Sorry, the Wi-Fi's a bit dodgy here.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: No problem, you're coming through fine. Thanks for getting in touch. How are you doing today?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Bit nervous, to be honest. I've been putting this call off for months.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: That's completely understandable. We'll go at your pace, and you can stop at any time.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Okay. Thanks.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Everything you tell me is confidential and covered by legal privilege. I'll make a note of our conversation. Is that alright?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Yeah, that's fine.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: In your email you said this is about your swimming coach when you were young.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Yeah. Brian Hollis. He ran the junior squad at Harbridge Swimming Club.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: And when did you start at the club?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: I joined when I was nine. He became my coach when I moved up to the squad at eleven.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Can you tell me, in your own words, what happened?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: He touched me. In the changing room, after training, when the others had gone.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Thank you. I know that's not easy to say.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Was there anything else he did?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Um. Yeah. This is the bit I've never really said out loud.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Take your time. There's no rush.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: He made me. He made me touch him.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Okay. Thank you.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: He said it was part of being in the squad. That everyone did it.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: How often did this happen?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Every Saturday. Saturday mornings after squad training.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: And over how long a period?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: About two years. From when I was eleven until I was nearly thirteen.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: So roughly 1996 to 1998?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Yeah, about then. It stopped when I quit swimming.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Did you tell anyone at the time?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: I told my mum when I was 13. She didn't really know what to do. She just took me out of the club.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Did she report it to anyone, as far as you know?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: No. I don't think so. We never talked about it again.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Who else have you told since?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: My wife, Claire, in 2020. Then my GP. And I went to the police last year, in March. I gave them a statement.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Do you know where the police investigation has got to?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: The officer said they've interviewed him. It's still ongoing.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Okay. Do you have the officer's name or a crime reference number?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Yeah, I've got it in an email. DC Farrow.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: That's helpful. Do you know whether anyone else was affected?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: I've heard he did it to other boys. A lad who was in the squad messaged me on Facebook and said he'd heard the same about a couple of others.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Did you see anything happen to anyone else yourself?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: No. I never saw anything. It's just what people have said.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Okay, thank you. Can I ask how all this has affected you?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: I've had anxiety for years. Panic attacks. I had counselling through work in 2021.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: And are you working at the moment?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Yeah, I'm a site manager. I had three months off sick in 2021, though.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Do you have anything from that time, letters, records?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: I've got the sick notes. And the counsellor wrote a letter for the police.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Good. So, what would you like to achieve from a claim?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: I want the club to admit it. I want them to say they let it happen. And, honestly, some money for the counselling, because the NHS waiting list is huge.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: That's helpful. Let me explain a few things. Normally there's a three-year time limit for personal injury claims, which for a child starts at eighteen.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: So I'm way past that?

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: In abuse cases the court can allow a claim to go ahead outside the time limit. It looks at things like why there was a delay and whether a fair trial is still possible. It's an important hurdle, but it's not the end of the road.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Right. Okay.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: The claim could be against Mr Hollis himself and against the club, if he was acting as their coach.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: The club's still going. Different people run it now.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: That's fine, it can still be responsible. On funding, we'd usually act on a no win, no fee agreement. I'll send you the details.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Okay, that's a relief.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: So, next steps. Could you send me the crime reference, DC Farrow's details, the counsellor's letter and the sick notes by Friday the 4th of December?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Yeah, I can do that.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: With your permission, I'll request your GP records. I'll send you a form to sign this week.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: That's fine.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: I'll also write to the police to ask about the investigation, and I'll send you our client care letter and the funding agreement by Monday the 30th.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: And please look after yourself. If you need support, the counsellor you saw or your GP are good places to start. I'll also send you details of a support service for survivors.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Thanks. It's a weight off, actually, saying it to someone who isn't family.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: You've done really well. Let's speak again on the 10th of December.

disclosures.what: Mr Kerr said his swimming coach, Brian Hollis, touched him in the changing room after training when the others had gone.
Mr Kerr said the coach made him touch him, saying it was part of being in the squad.
Mr Kerr said this happened every Saturday after squad training for about two years, from when he was eleven.
Mr Kerr said he told his mum at thirteen, who took him out of the club, and later his wife, his GP and the police, to whom he gave a statement last March.
